questions.stem: Who is associated with 'nudge theory'?
questions.passage_context:
Behavioural economics has reshaped policy thinking globally. Founded on the recognition that humans consistently deviate from the 'rational economic agent' assumed by classical theory, the field draws on psychology to explain real-world decisions. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky's pioneering work on heuristics and biases laid the foundation; Richard Thaler's 'nudge theory' translated insights into practical policy design. The 2017 Nobel Prize to Thaler recognised this paradigm shift.

In India, behavioural economics finds rich application. Aadhaar-enabled Direct Benefit Transfers harness default choices to ensure subsidy reach. The 'Give it Up' campaign for LPG subsidy, encouraging well-off households to voluntarily forgo subsidy, demonstrated how social proof and identity-framing can drive voluntary action. Over 1.13 crore consumers gave up their subsidies — a remarkably effective behavioural intervention.

Banking and finance have been particularly fertile ground. Auto-debit mandates exploit inertia: once set, people rarely cancel. SIP (Systematic Investment Plan) subscriptions have benefited from this — over ₹20,000 crore monthly is now invested through SIPs. RBI's 'Reflexive Asks' framework, which prompts customers about potential overdraft fees before transactions, has reduced inadvertent charges.

Yet behavioural insights have limits. They work best for individual choices in stable contexts; they're less effective for systemic problems requiring institutional reform. Critics also caution against paternalism — policymakers nudging citizens toward 'good' decisions without explicit consent raises ethical questions about agency and autonomy.

Looking ahead, the integration of behavioural economics with digital tools — recommendations engines, gamification, smart defaults — promises to amplify impact. The challenge will be balancing effectiveness with transparency: ensuring that 'nudges' genuinely serve citizens' long-term interests rather than commercial or political agendas.
questions.explanation: **Richard Thaler** — Nobel laureate 2017 — pioneered 'nudge theory' in his book of the same name with Cass Sunstein.
questions.subject: ENGLISH

8 friends in a row facing North.
1. P at extreme left. 2. Q is 4th from P's right.
3. R between P and Q. 4. S imm right of Q.
5. T between S and U.
6. U at pos 8 (extreme right). 7. V at pos 3.

**Final:** P(1), W(2)?, V(3), Q(4)?, R between P and Q so R at 2, V at 3 conflict. Adjusting:
Take Q at pos 5 (4th from P=1 right means 4 positions to the right: pos 5). R between P(1) and Q(5) at pos 2, 3, or 4. V at pos 3. So R at pos 2 or 4.
S imm right of Q ⟹ S at pos 6. T between S(6) and U(8) ⟹ T at pos 7.
Remaining: W at pos 4 (or wherever R isn't). Try R at pos 2: P(1), R(2), V(3), W(4), Q(5), S(6), T(7), U(8). All conditions ✓.
**Final:** P(1), R(2), V(3), W(4), Q(5), S(6), T(7), U(8).
